title: With Due Respect (Vol. 4) -- Ch. 10: Tread Cautiously and Prudently
keywords: a mere interlocutory order... immediately executory
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4) -- CJP's February 27, 2011 Inquirer column advising the House Committee on Justice that it could resume the impeachment of Ombudsman Merceditas Gutierrez (suspended by a Supreme Court status quo ante order) but should 'tread cautiously and prudently' through a maze of conflicting opinions

His point that the lifting of the status quo ante order took effect immediately -- because that order was 'a mere interlocutory order,' and a court may lift such an order 'with immediate effect' -- so the committee need not wait for finality to resume

His map of the fractured Court: the splintered reasons among the nine-justice majority (Del Castillo and Perez, Nachura's 'prematurity,' Abad's articles-in-the-Senate view) and Justice Brion's dissent (joined by four) that the committee acted before the impeachment Rules were published and thus violated Gutierrez's due process

His prudent advice -- to 'forestall any possible flip-flops and delays,' heed Brion's suggested remedy by taking 'a new vote on... sufficiency in form and substance' and giving the Ombudsman 'a fresh period of 15 days' -- noting that, unlike Francisco v. House (2003), this Court gave 'no clear answer' on when an impeachment is 'initiated'
sub_topics: The setup: CJP had written that the House Committee on Justice could 'immediately resume' the Gutierrez impeachment that the Court's status quo ante order had suspended; while a decision becomes final 15 days after receipt (and a motion for reconsideration can delay finality), the order to lift the status quo ante was different

Immediate effect: the status quo ante order was 'a mere interlocutory order' effective at once on September 14, 2010, so the order lifting it (written into the Court's decision) 'should also be deemed immediately executory,' since 'a court may lift an interlocutory order with immediate effect'

The caution: even so, the committee 'would be well advised to tread cautiously and prudently,' because the way forward is 'full of legal minefields laid down by the conflicting opinions of the justices'

The fractured majority: of the nine majority justices, two (Del Castillo and Perez) 'allowed only the first complaint but not the second'; Justice Nachura voted to dismiss solely on 'prematurity' (Gutierrez should first go to the committee); and Justice Abad voted to dismiss on the view that the one-year bar 'begins only when the House files the articles of impeachment in the Senate'

The Brion dissent: Justice Arturo Brion (joined unqualifiedly by four others) reasoned that when the committee found the complaints 'sufficient in form and substance,' the impeachment Rules 'had not been published and were thus not yet effective' -- they were published September 2, 2010 and took effect September 17 -- so the committee's pre-effectivity declarations were 'void for violating the due process rights of Gutierrez'

Brion's remedy: since the published Rules were now effective, nothing should prevent the House from 'resuming its proceedings from its last valid action' -- the Speaker's referral of the complaints to the Justice Committee

The prudent advice: to 'forestall any possible flip-flops and delays on reconsideration,' the committee could heed Brion, 'take a new vote on the issue of sufficiency in form and substance,' and then 're-direct the Ombudsman to answer within a fresh period of 15 days' -- and Brion's view on when impeachment is 'initiated' (only when the committee gets its 'first opportunity for a meaningful action') is 'not disadvantageous' to the committee

The bottom line: a 'strong majority' dismissed the Gutierrez petition 'for different reasons,' so unlike Francisco v. House of Representatives (2003) the Court had 'no clear answer' on when an impeachment is 'initiated' -- only four justices (Carpio, Morales, Villarama, Mendoza) sustained the Francisco rule, while five dissenters (Corona, De Castro, Brion, Peralta, Bersamin) put the trigger at the committee's sufficiency finding (Velasco inhibited) -- so the committee must 'tiptoe its way in the maze of these labyrinthine opinions'

notable_anecdotes: Interlocutory, so immediate: CJP's key technical point -- the status quo ante order took effect at once on September 14, 2010, so lifting it is just as immediately executory.

A 5-4-and-scattered Court: he tallies the splintered votes -- only four justices clearly sustaining Francisco v. House on when impeachment is 'initiated,' five dissenters putting the trigger elsewhere, and one (Velasco) inhibiting.

Rules published too late: he highlights Brion's reasoning that the impeachment Rules took effect only September 17, 2010, after the committee had already acted -- voiding those actions for want of due process.
'Tiptoe... the maze': he closes by urging the committee to step carefully through the 'labyrinthine opinions,' taking a fresh vote to avoid future flip-flops.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's February 27, 2011 Inquirer column, advises the House Committee on Justice that it could resume the impeachment of Ombudsman Merceditas Gutierrez -- suspended by the Supreme Court's status quo ante order -- but should 'tread cautiously and prudently.' His threshold point is technical: while a decision becomes final 15 days after receipt (and a motion for reconsideration can delay finality), the status quo ante order was 'a mere interlocutory order' effective at once on September 14, 2010, so the order lifting it (written into the Court's decision) 'should also be deemed immediately executory,' since 'a court may lift an interlocutory order with immediate effect.' Even so, the way forward is 'full of legal minefields laid down by the conflicting opinions of the justices.' He maps the fracture: of the nine-justice majority, two (Del Castillo and Perez) allowed only the first complaint; Nachura would dismiss on 'prematurity'; and Abad thought the one-year bar 'begins only when the House files the articles of impeachment in the Senate.' Justice Brion's dissent (joined by four) reasoned that when the committee found the complaints 'sufficient in form and substance,' the impeachment Rules 'had not been published and were thus not yet effective' (published September 2, effective September 17), so the committee's declarations were 'void for violating the due process rights of Gutierrez' -- but Brion offered a remedy: resume from 'the last valid action,' the Speaker's referral to the Justice Committee. CJP's prudent counsel: to 'forestall any possible flip-flops and delays,' the committee should take 'a new vote on... sufficiency in form and substance' and give the Ombudsman 'a fresh period of 15 days.' He stresses that, unlike Francisco v. House of Representatives (2003), this Court gave 'no clear answer' on when an impeachment is 'initiated' -- only four justices (Carpio, Morales, Villarama, Mendoza) sustained the Francisco rule, while five dissenters (Corona, De Castro, Brion, Peralta, Bersamin) put the trigger at the committee's sufficiency finding, and Velasco inhibited -- so the committee must 'tiptoe its way in the maze of these labyrinthine opinions.'
